'''Robert John Ferrier''' FRSNZ,<ref name="List of Fellows">{{cite web|title=List of Fellows|url=http://www.royalsociety.org.nz/organisation/academy/fellowship/fellows-1919-present/d-f/|publisher=Royal Society of New Zealand|accessdate=23 April 2014}}</ref> FNZIC,<ref name="NZIC obituary" /> (7 August 1932 – 11 July 2013) was an organic chemist who discovered two chemical reactions, the [[Ferrier rearrangement]] and the [[Ferrier carbocyclization]].<ref name="Ferrier 1979 1455–1458">{{cite journal|last=Ferrier|first=Robert J|title=Unsaturated Carbohydrates. Part 21. A Carboxylic Ring Closure of a Hex-5-enopyranoside Derivative|journal=J. Chem. Soc. Perkin Trans.|date=1979|volume=1|pages=1455–1458|doi=10.1039/P19790001455}}</ref><ref name="Blattner 1986 151–162">{{cite journal|last=Blattner|first=RJ|author2=Ferrier RJ |title=Direct synthesis of 6-oxabicyclo[3.2.1]octane derivatives from deoxyinososes|journal=Carbohydr. Res.|date=1986|volume=150|pages=151–162|doi=10.1016/0008-6215(86)80012-X}}</ref> Originally from Edinburgh, he moved to Wellington, New Zealand, in 1970.

== Early life and education ==

Ferrier was born in [[Edinburgh]] on 7 August 1932. Following the family's idiosyncratic naming tradition, although he was named Robert John, he was always known as Robin. Likewise his father Edward was known as William and his mother Sophia was known as Rita. William was a policeman and became head of Edinburgh CID, while Rita was a housewife.

His only sibling was a [[fraternal twin]] sister Dr [[Barbara M. Ferrier]] (d. 2006), known as Ray, who likewise became an organic chemist, becoming professor emeritus of the Department of Biochemistry and Biomedical Sciences at [[McMaster University]].<ref>[http://fhs.mcmaster.ca/main/news/news_archives/ferrier.htm A tribute to professor emeritus Barbara Ferrier] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170102000000/https://web.archive.org/web/20170102112327/http://fhs.mcmaster.ca/main/news/news_archives/ferrier.htm |date=2 January 2017 }}, McMaster University, 6 January 2006</ref>  A [[polycyclic compound|polycyclic]] [[ketone]] "barbaralone", related to [[Bullvalene#Barbaralane|bullvalene]] was named after her.<ref>Alex Nickon, Ernest F. Silversmith, ''Organic Chemistry: The Name Game: Modern Coined Terms and Their Origins'', [https://books.google.com/books?id=1jb9BAAAQBAJ&pg=PA133 p. 133], Pergamon Press, 1987.</ref>

Ferrier attended [[George Heriot's School]] for all of his schooling, apart from a brief time in Traquair, to where he was evacuated during the war with his mother and sister.

He gained a Bachelor of Science with first class honours in 1954 and a PhD in plant [[polysaccharides]] in 1957, under Professor Gerald Aspinall.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Aspinall|first=G.O.|author2=Ferrier, R. J. |title=The constitution of barley-husk hemicellulose|journal=Journal of the Chemical Society|date=1957|pages=4188–4194|doi=10.1039/jr9570004188 }}</ref>

== Academic career ==

Appointed to a teaching position at [[Birkbeck College]], University of London, Ferrier's focus turned from [[polysaccharides]] to [[monosaccharides]]. New laboratory tools and methods enabled their reactions and mechanisms to be studied like normal organic compounds, rather than a separate field, and he pioneered this approach.<ref name="NZIC obituary">{{cite journal|last=Wilcox|first=Sarah|author2=Furneaux, Richard |title=Obituary Robert John (Robin) Ferrier|journal=Chemistry in New Zealand|date=2013|volume=October|url=http://nzic.org.nz/CiNZ/articles/2013/CiNZ%20Oct%202013%20Obit_Ferrier.pdf}}</ref> In the early 1960s as a NATO Post Doctoral Fellow, he worked in Professor [[Melvin Calvin]]’s group at the [[University of California, Berkeley]]. They were exciting times. While Ferrier was there, Calvin was awarded the [[Nobel Prize for Chemistry]],<ref>{{cite web|last=Calvin|first=Melvin|title=The Nobel Prize in Chemistry 1961|url=https://www.nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/chemistry/laureates/1961/|work=Nobelprize.org|accessdate=23 April 2014}}</ref> and he also met Carolyn Tompkins, the pair marrying in Edinburgh in 1962.

Arriving in New Zealand in 1970 as [[Birkbeck College, University of London|Victoria University’s]] first chair of organic chemistry,<ref>{{cite book|last=Barrowman|first=Rachel|title=Victoria University of Wellington, 1899-1999: A History|date=1999|publisher=Victoria University Press}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last=Halton|first=Brian|authorlink=Brian Halton|title=Chemistry at Victoria The Wellington University A Personalized Account of the Hundred Years from 1899|date=2014|publisher=The School of Chemical & Physical Sciences, Victoria University of Wellington|pages=53–54|url=http://www.victoria.ac.nz/scps/about/attachments/ChemHist_second-edition_lowres.pdf}}</ref> Ferrier continued to lead work on the monosaccharides, specialising in their use as starting materials for the synthesis of non-carbohydrate compounds of pharmaceutical interest. He had previously clarified the mechanism of the Fischer glycosidation and discovered an allylic rearrangement reaction of glycals, now known as the [[Ferrier rearrangement]]<ref name="Ferrier 1979 1455–1458"/><ref name="Blattner 1986 151–162"/>  – the first of two reactions that bear his name. Many of Ferrier's best discoveries were made by following up unexpected chemical observations, which often led him into uncharted territory. His second ‘name’ reaction, the [[Ferrier carbocyclization]], was the result of this approach.

He served on the Toxic Substances Board in the 1980s and the leadership of the [[RSNZ]] report ''Lead in the Environment''<ref>{{cite journal|last=Ferrier|first=R.J.|author2=Davies RB |author3=Edwards IR |author4=Fergusson DM |author5=Reeves RD |author6=Scott PJ |author7=Stevenson CD |title=Lead in the Environment in New Zealand|journal=The Royal Society of New Zealand (Miscellaneous Series)|date=1986|volume=14|pages=130}}</ref> that confirmed the toxic effects of lead and began the phase-out of leaded petrol.

After his retirement from Victoria University in 1998, he became an emeritus professor.<ref>{{cite book|title=Calendar|date=2000|publisher=Victoria University of Wellington|pages=15|url=http://www.victoria.ac.nz/about/publications/calendar/calendar_2001.pdf}}</ref> Ferrier then entered what he referred to as his 'supposed retirement', working with the carbohydrate chemists at [[Industrial Research Ltd]]. Here he continued to foster the next generation of carbohydrate chemists in New Zealand – his 'grandchildren', instilling his rigorous approach to chemistry with mentoring and assistance with the group's publications.<ref>{{cite web|title=American Chemical Society Division of Carbohydrate Chemistry|url=http://carb.sites.acs.org/pdfs/Newsletters/CARBNewsletterFall2013.pdf|work=Newsletter Fall 2013|accessdate=23 April 2014}}</ref>

== Ferrier Research Institute ==
The Ferrier Research Institute at [[Victoria University of Wellington]] was named for Ferrier. It was created on 6 January 2014 to accommodate the group of carbohydrate chemists who left [[Callaghan Innovation]] on that date. (Callaghan Innovation was previously [[Industrial Research Ltd]].)

== Ferrier Lecture ==

In August 2012, Ferrier celebrated his 80th birthday and retired a second time. Later that year, the Ferrier Trust was set up in his honour, to bring a scientist to New Zealand each year, to engage with chemistry students and lecture. Peppi Prasit, a Ferrier PhD graduate and founder of Amira Pharmaceuticals and Inception Sciences in the US, was the trust's foundation donor. He was able to attend the inaugural Ferrier Lecture in March 2013.<ref>{{cite web|title=School of Chemical and Physical Sciences, Victoria University of Wellington|url=http://www.victoria.ac.nz/scps/about/news/2013-news#a173730|accessdate=23 April 2014}}</ref>

== Publications ==

In his 50-year career, Ferrier published 180 papers, reviews and books, and gave 10 invited plenary lectures at international symposia.<ref>A full list of publications is available from the [http://www.royalsociety.org.nz/organisation/academy/fellowship/obituaries/robert-john-robin-ferrier/ Royal Society of New Zealand website].</ref> His reviews were of particular benefit to the chemical community but perhaps of most value was the book "Monosaccharide Chemistry,<ref>{{cite book|last=Ferrier|first=R.J.|title=Monosaccharide Chemistry|date=1972|publisher=Penguin|location=Hammondsworth|author2=Collins, P.M. |oclc=9225402}}</ref> written with Dr Peter Collins in 1972 and majorly updated as "Monosaccharides: Their chemistry and their roles in natural products<ref>{{cite book|last=Ferrier|first=R.J.|title=Monosaccharides: Their chemistry and their roles in natural products|date=1995|publisher=Wiley & Sons|location=Chichester, New York|author2=Collins, P.M. |oclc=30894482}}</ref> in 1995.

== Awards ==

Ferrier was elected [[Fellow of the Royal Society of New Zealand]] (1977)<ref name="List of Fellows"/> and the New Zealand Institute of Chemistry (1972) and awarded a DSc (London, 1968).<ref>{{cite web|publisher=Royal Society of New Zealand|title=Robert John (Robin) Ferrier|url=https://www.royalsociety.org.nz/who-we-are/our-people/our-fellows/obituaries/fellows-obituaries/robert-john-robin-ferrier/|accessdate=7 March 2013}}</ref>
